submission.natural_language_explanation: GPT-2 L1/N277's pre-activation is pinned in the flat basin around the GELU minimum (x = -0.753, where the activation bottoms out at -0.17004, exactly this pole's scan maximum, 0.17004072666168213), because the neuron reads the block-0 attention output - the mixed left context - rather than the current token's identity. The negative pole is therefore a near-constant GELU-floor readout, not a content detector: predicted active (peak 0.65-1.00 x scale, 0.87-1.00 for ordinary text) for any prompt of two or more tokens whatever the topic, language or token identity, and predicted inactive (peak <= 0.16 x scale) only for a one-token prompt; within a sequence its strength decays smoothly with absolute position (pre-activation crosses zero near position 90 and turns positive beyond, where the same neuron's positive pole fires), so a long sequence loses the pole after roughly 80 tokens even though the peak over a prompt is always set by its early tokens.

adversarial_test_results.detail: The hypothesis's own claimed trigger token, but as a one-token prompt; the hypothesis says the pole is active only for two or more tokens and predicts a peak at or below 0.16 x scale here.
A second claimed activating token isolated as a one-token prompt; the hypothesis predicts the trigger word alone cannot fire the pole without at least one preceding token.
A third claimed peak token as a complete one-token prompt; the hypothesis predicts the one-token regime caps activation at 0.16 x scale regardless of which token it is.
An ordinary single word with no claimed trigger; the hypothesis predicts inactivity for every one-token prompt, so this tests that the inactive regime is not specific to the trigger tokens.
A lone high-frequency function word occupying only the first position, a classic massive-activation site; the hypothesis still predicts a one-token prompt stays at or below 0.16 x scale.
A single pronoun token, one of the shortest possible non-empty prompts; the hypothesis predicts the GELU-floor readout needs a second token to engage, so this should be inactive.

A single concrete noun token with no grammar around it; if the pole needed any real lexical content rather than merely two tokens, this would be the place it shows, but the hypothesis predicts inactivity.
A second single common-noun token from a different word class than the trigger tokens; the hypothesis predicts it remains in the one-token inactive regime at or below 0.16 x scale.
A one-token numeral prompt, a token class absent from the top examples; the hypothesis's token-count rule says one token is still one token, so it predicts inactivity.
A single punctuation token with no lexical or syntactic content; the hypothesis predicts any one-token prompt is inactive, so this should be at most 0.16 x scale.
A lone period, the most frequent token in running text but still only one token; the hypothesis predicts the pole does not fire on it in isolation.

A lone delimiter character, the closest one-token near-miss to top example 2's '><' peak; the hypothesis attributes the HTML example's activation to its left context, not the delimiter, so it predicts inactivity here.

The shortest natural two-token prompt I can construct; the hypothesis's sharp threshold claim says two tokens suffice, so it predicts activation in the 0.65-1.00 x scale band rather than the one-token regime.

Four punctuation tokens with no words at all; the hypothesis says the pole is not a content detector and fires on any prompt of two or more tokens, so it predicts activation here despite the absence of lexical content.
Gibberish subword tokens in no language; the hypothesis claims token-identity independence, so it predicts this meaningless multi-token prompt is still active.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Papermaking is generally traced to the Han court official Cai Lun, who is said to have presented a process for making paper from tree bark, hemp waste, rags and old fishing nets around the year 105. Earlier fragments of coarse paper have been found in northern China, so the attribution is probably an oversimplification of a longer development. From China the technique travelled slowly westward along trade routes, reaching Korea and Japan within a few centuries and the Islamic world by the eighth century, where mills in Baghdad, Damascus and later Fez produced sheets in quantities that supported large administrative and scholarly communities. European paper mills appeared in Spain and Italy during the thirteenth century; the earliest surviving records describe water-driven stamping hammers that reduced linen rags to a pulp, which was then formed on wire screens, pressed and hung to dry in lofts. Because rags were the principal raw material, paper production remained tied for centuries to the supply of worn textiles, and shortages repeatedly prompted experiments with substitutes such as straw, bamboo, mulberry bark and eventually wood pulp, whose adoption in the nineteenth century transformed the economics of printing. The introduction of the Fourdrinier machine in the early eighteen hundreds allowed a continuous web of paper to be formed, pressed and dried in a single sequence, replacing the batch process of individual moulds. Industrial chemistry followed, supplying sizing agents, mineral fillers such as clay and calcium carbonate, and bleaching methods that changed both the appearance and the durability of the finished sheet. Conservation research in the twentieth century showed that acidic sizing was a major cause of embrittlement in library collections, which led to standardized archival papers with alkaline reserves and to routine testing of tear resistance and folding endurance. Modern mills recycle a substantial share of their fibre, and the measurement of fibre length, freeness and ash content remains central to quality control. Historians of technology note that the sequence of small improvements in screening, pressing and drying is often more consequential than any single invention, and that surviving documents tell us as much about the economics of their manufacture as about the events they record. Read as a whole, the surviving samples suggest a craft that changed gradually and unevenly, with regional workshops adopting new tools only when local supplies of rags, water power and skilled labour made them worthwhile.
